Onboarding Guide

Connect Quarri to Microsoft 365 Copilot

Add Quarri to Copilot Studio as an MCP tool, and make it available to your team in Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams. Requires a Microsoft work or school account with Copilot Studio access.

Admin Setup
Build the Agent in Copilot Studio
An administrator or maker with Copilot Studio access carries out these steps once. Individual users do not repeat them — but each user does sign in to Quarri with their own account the first time they use the agent.
1
Open Copilot Studio
Go to copilotstudio.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft work or school account. A personal Microsoft account will not work.
2
Create an Agent
On the home screen, select Agent under “Optimize your business processes”. Name it Quarri. If you are prompted to describe the agent conversationally, skip that and configure it directly.
3
Set the Model to Claude Opus 5
In the right-hand panel, set Model to Claude Opus 5. Quarri is built and tested against Claude, so this gives noticeably better tool selection and query construction than the default model.
4
Open Channels
In the right-hand panel, select Channels to define where users will interact with the agent.
5
Add the Teams + Microsoft 365 Channel
Choose Teams + Microsoft 365.
6
Choose Where the Agent Appears
Select Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Teams, then press Add channel.

This choice is permanent

The availability setting cannot be changed after publishing. If you are unsure, “Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Teams” is the broadest option and covers both surfaces.

7
Open Tools
Back in the right-hand panel, select Tools — this is where the agent connects to external systems.
8
Add a New Tool
In the Add a tool dialog, ignore the featured connectors and press the + Add button in the top right.
9
Select Model Context Protocol
From the dropdown, choose Model Context Protocol (MCP).

MCP, not Connectors

The Connectors tab builds a Power Platform custom connector from an OpenAPI schema by hand. It reaches the same place but is far more work, and it does not offer the automatic authentication setup used in the next steps.

10
Enter the Quarri Server Details
Fill in the server details, set Authentication to OAuth 2.0 and Configuration type to Dynamic (with discovery), then press Add.
Server name: Quarri
Server URL: https://app.quarri.ai/mcp
Authentication: OAuth 2.0
Configuration type: Dynamic (with discovery)

Write a useful server description

Copilot’s orchestrator reads this description to decide when to call Quarri. Something specific — for example “Query unified business data across sales, operations and finance in natural language” — works considerably better than just “Quarri”.

11
Create a Connection
The connection shows as Not connected. Open the dropdown beside it.
12
Choose Create New Connection
Select Create new connection.
13
Confirm the Connection
Leave the display name as Quarri and press Create.
14
Authorise Access to Quarri
A Quarri sign-in window opens. Check you are signed in as the right user, then press Allow Access.

If this screen mentions Claude

The consent screen may refer to Claude or Claude Desktop. This is a labelling issue on the Quarri authorisation page and does not affect what you are connecting — the permissions granted and the data accessed are exactly as listed on that screen.

15
Confirm and Add
The connection now shows Quarri with a green indicator. Press Add to attach it to your agent.
16
Turn On Memory
Quarri now appears under Tools. Scroll to the bottom of the right-hand panel and switch Memory on, so the agent keeps context across a conversation rather than re-deriving it with every question.
17
Publish
Press Publish in the top right. Publishing makes the agent live — but it does not yet make it visible to your colleagues. See the next section.
Rollout
Making Quarri Available to Your Team
Publishing and appearing in Copilot chat are two different things. After you publish, the agent enters an approval queue before anyone else can see it.
→
What Happens Next
The published agent is submitted for review in the Microsoft 365 admin centre or Teams admin centre. An IT administrator reviews the agent’s name, description and the connectors it uses, then approves or declines it.

Once approved, Quarri appears in the Agent Store under Built by your org, and the administrator decides who gets access — either assigning it to named users and groups, or pushing it out organisation-wide. From there it is available in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Teams, Outlook, Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

What your IT team will want to know

Authentication is per user. Every person signs in to Quarri with their own account and sees a consent prompt the first time. There is no shared service account.

Access controls still apply. Quarri resolves team filters, row-level permissions and tenant restrictions from each user’s own token, so people see exactly what they are entitled to see and no more.

Queries are attributable. Quarri’s audit trail records activity against real named users.

Data policies apply. The connection runs over Power Platform connectors, so any DLP policy governing connectors in that environment also governs Quarri.

→
A Note on Copilot Credits
Copilot Studio meters agent activity against your tenant’s Copilot Credits, including testing in the preview pane. If the environment has no credits allocated, the agent stops responding and returns an EnforcementUsageCredits error. Credits can be reallocated from another environment, bought as a capacity pack, or billed as you go by linking an Azure subscription in the Power Platform admin centre.
Before You Begin
What to Expect
An honest account of where this integration stands today.
!
Quarri in Copilot Is Lightly Tested
We have verified the connection, the authentication flow and the security model, but Quarri has not yet been through sustained real-world use inside Copilot. Expect rough edges, and please tell us when you hit them.

Three things are worth knowing up front.

The tool surface is large. Quarri exposes well over a hundred tools. Copilot’s orchestrator picks among them from a single server description, and it will not always pick well. This shows up most on complex, multi-step questions.

Saved skills do not carry over cleanly. Quarri’s skills — saved procedures that encode how to answer a recurring question correctly — are built around a workflow that Copilot’s orchestrator does not follow in the same way.

Every interaction costs credits, including the ones that go nowhere.
★
Our Recommendation: Use Claude
Copilot is a reasonable way to put Quarri in front of people who already live in Teams and Outlook, and for straightforward lookups it works well. For anyone doing real analytical work, Claude is a materially better experience today:

•  Quarri is built and tested against Claude first, so its behaviour there is the most predictable
•  Claude handles the full tool surface natively, including the ordered workflow Quarri expects — find the saved skill, load the schema, resolve the filter values, then query
•  Saved skills work as designed, which is what makes recurring questions reliably correct
•  Richer output — charts, dashboards and documents rather than chat text
•  No per-interaction metering against a tenant credit pool

The two are not mutually exclusive. Run Quarri in Copilot for quick lookups in the flow of work, and in Claude for analysis.
